{{Short description|Scottish mathematician and expert in electricity}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=October 2017}}
{{Use British English|date=October 2017}}

'''James Douglas Hamilton Dickson''' [[FRSE]] [[Royal Institution|MRI]] (1 May 1849 – 6 February 1931) was a Scottish mathematician and expert in electricity. He was a Senior  Fellow at [[Peterhouse, Cambridge]]. Glasgow University elected him an Eglinton Fellow. He was the elder brother of [[Charles Dickson, Lord Dickson]].<ref name="whowaswho">''Who Was Who'', 2014: J D H Dickson.</ref>

He had in-depth knowledge in fields of electricity and electrostatics and also a great interest in low temperature physics.

==Life==
{{More citations needed|section|date=January 2023}}
He was born in [[Glasgow]] on 1 May 1849, a son of Dr John Robert Dickson of [[Edinburgh]]. He attended both [[Glasgow University|Glasgow]] and [[Cambridge University|Cambridge]] Universities, graduating MA. From 1867 to 1869 he was assistant to [[William Thomson, Lord Kelvin]], being the joint-builder of the technical equipment which Kelvin used to measure electrostatic energy. In 1869, he assisted Kelvin in the laying of the first Transatlantic communication cables. The French company overseeing the work were impressed by Dickson and kept him in their employ as Electrician-in-Charge, based in [[Brest, France|Brest]] until 1870.<ref name="whowaswho"/>

He returned to Cambridge to collaborate with W H King and Theophillus Varley in creating more of Lord Kelvin's machines, including the siphon recorder.
In 1877 he became a Maths Tutor at [[Peterhouse, Cambridge|Peterhouse]], his alma mater. In 1907 the college made him a Senior Fellow. He was later made a Governor of the college. He was also a Governor of [[Huntingdon Grammar School]].{{cn|date=March 2024}}

He was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]] in 1876. His proposers were Sir [[James Dewar]] (his brother-in-law), [[Peter Guthrie Tait]], [[Alexander Crum Brown]], and [[William Turner (anatomist)|William Turner]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Biographical Index of Former Fellows of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 1783–2002|date=July 2006|publisher=The Royal Society of Edinburgh|isbn=0-902-198-84-X|url=https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp1.pdf|access-date=12 February 2016|archive-date=24 January 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130124115814/http://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp1.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

During the [[First World War]], at which point he was officially retired, he was asked to fill in for absent masters teaching Maths at both [[Fettes College]] and [[Edinburgh Academy]].

He died on 6 February 1931, aged 81.

==Publications==
Over and above multiple papers on mathematics and physics, Dickson enjoyed biographical work. Three entries in the Dictionary of National Biography are under his authorship:<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Author:James_Douglas_Hamilton_Dickson|title = James Douglas Hamilton Dickson - Wikisource, the free online library}}</ref>
*[[Peter Guthrie Tait]]
*[[Edward John Routh]]

==Family==

He married Isobel Catherine Banks, sister of his sister-in-law Hestor Bagot Banks (i.e. the two brothers married two sisters). A third sister, Helen Rose Banks, married Sir [[James Dewar]], connecting all three figures.
